title: 50 Renderings and Not One Shows the Buyer's Unit: Why Density Wins
seoTitle: 50 Renderings, Zero Units: Show the Buyer's Own View
description: Why a presale with 50 renderings of the lobby and pool still leaves buyers unsure, and why one image of their own unit and view sells more.
answer: Most presale projects show 50 renderings of the lobby, the pool, the penthouse and the rooftop, and not one of the unit the buyer is actually buying. Those images are beautiful but useless to the buyer on the 8th floor. Density beats quantity: one image of their own view, from their own unit, sells more than 50 generic renderings.
body:
Open almost any presale website and count the renderings. Twenty, thirty, sometimes fifty. Then ask a simple question: how many of them show the unit the buyer is about to buy? In my experience, the answer is usually zero.

## What the typical rendering package shows

The usual set looks the same everywhere:

- The lobby
- The pool
- The penthouse
- The rooftop

They are beautiful. A lot of money and talent went into them. And for most buyers, they are useless.

## Why beautiful renderings do not help most buyers

Think about the buyer on the 8th floor. He is not buying the penthouse. He is not buying the rooftop view. He is buying one specific unit, on one specific floor, facing one specific direction.

When every image shows a space he will never own, he still has no answer to the questions that matter to him. What will I see from my window? How will my living room feel? The more generic images you add, the more obvious it becomes that his unit is missing from the story.

A penthouse image does not sell a one-bedroom on a low floor. It only shows the buyer what he is not getting.

## Density beats quantity

The fix is not more renderings. It is more relevant ones. I call this density over quantity: fewer images, each one closer to the decision the buyer is making.

One image of the buyer's own view, from his own unit, does more work than fifty pictures of shared spaces. It answers his real question. It lets him picture himself living there. And it removes the doubt that makes him wait.

## How to check your own marketing

Here is a simple test you can run on your project today:

1. Count every rendering you use in your marketing.
2. Mark the ones that show a real unit a buyer can actually purchase.
3. Mark the ones that show the real view from a specific floor and side.
4. Compare those numbers with the total.

If most of your images are amenities and the penthouse, your marketing is speaking to a small part of your buyers. The rest are left to guess.

## The bottom line

Renderings are not the problem. Spending the whole budget on the same spaces is. Show each buyer the unit and the view they are actually considering, and one image will do more than fifty.
takeaways: Most presale rendering packages show the lobby, pool, penthouse and rooftop, but not the units buyers are buying.
Generic images are beautiful but useless for a buyer on a lower floor.
Density beats quantity: relevant images matter more than a large number of images.
One image of a buyer's own view from their own unit sells more than 50 generic renderings.
Count how many of your renderings show a real unit to see who your marketing is really speaking to.
faq: How many renderings does a presale project need?
There is no magic number. What matters is how many of them show the units and views buyers are actually choosing between, not the total count.
Why do penthouse renderings not sell regular units?
Because the buyer of a one-bedroom on a low floor is not buying that view or that space. The image shows him what he is not getting instead of what he is.
What image helps a presale buyer decide?
An image of the view from his own unit, on his own floor and side. It answers the question he is really asking and helps him picture living there.
Are amenity renderings a waste of money?
Not entirely, but they should not be the whole package. If almost none of your images show a real unit, most of your buyers are left guessing.
